title: Somalia: The Journalists Who Disappeared
content:
In October 2022, Abdalle Ahmed Mumin — Secretary-General of the Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS), the organisation that documents what happens to journalists in Somalia — arrived at Aden Adde International Airport in Mogadishu carrying a ticket to Nairobi. He was travelling to seek medical care for injuries he had sustained during a previous detention.

He did not make his flight. According to documentation by the SJS and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), NISA officers detained him at the departure gate without a warrant, without stated charges, and without notifying his family or his organisation of where he was being taken. His apparent offence: he had issued a press statement ten days earlier expressing concern that a new government media directive was worded so broadly it would suppress legitimate journalism — and he had refused to retract it.

This was his first arrest. He was released, then arrested again when he attempted to travel for medical care. In February 2023, according to the SJS and RFK Human Rights, NISA officers detained him a third time. In his own public statements, as documented by the CPJ, he has said officers told him they would kill him if he resisted. According to the SJS and his own public account, he was held for thirty-three days and subjected to treatment that he has publicly described as torture. He was eventually released. Days later, as recounted by the SJS and IPI, a court order froze the SJS bank accounts, but no NISA officer involved in any of the three detentions was investigated, disciplined, or prosecuted.

Abdalle Ahmed Mumin returned to his desk.

“If I stop, they have won. If enough of us stop, there is no press left.”

— Abdalle Ahmed Mumin, Secretary-General, Somali Journalists Syndicate

That return — that refusal to stop — captures something about Somalia’s press freedom crisis that the international community is not fully seeing. The dominant narrative focuses on the journalists killed: seventy-three since the civil war began, according to the CPJ, with not one killing producing a conviction, according to CPJ records. That story is real and must be told. But alongside it, and increasingly supplanting it, runs a different and in some ways more calculated story: Somalia’s security apparatus has learned that arresting journalists is cheap, quiet, and equally effective.

Between 2007 and 2013, Al-Shabaab’s campaign against Somalia’s press was built on murder. Eighteen journalists were killed in 2012 alone — the highest single-year figure recorded in any country since. The killings generated international condemnation, press freedom resources, and diplomatic pressure. They were visible. Visibility, as those responsible eventually discovered, has costs.

The arrest figures tell the rest of the story. The SJS documented six journalist arrests by state security forces in 2015. By 2019, that figure had reached thirty-eight — a record, with thirty-seven journalists also beaten or threatened at gunpoint that year, predominantly by state forces rather than Al-Shabaab, according to the SJS. Between March and May 2025, the SJS and CPJ documented forty-one journalists arrested, assaulted, or harassed in sixty days. The International Press Institute (IPI) documented at least eighteen press freedom violations in Somalia in the second half of 2025 — among the highest totals recorded on the continent that period.

An overnight detention rarely makes international news. Confiscating footage, forcing a retraction, or freezing an organisation’s bank accounts achieves the same silencing effect as a death threat — at a fraction of the diplomatic cost. The journalist is silenced. The world does not notice. The officer who conducted the arrest faces no consequence.

Working as a human rights practitioner based in Mogadishu, I have observed alongside how detention is used as press suppression in Somalia, as has also been documented extensively by the SJS, the CPJ, and the US State Department. The patterns are consistent: arrest after publication to punish specific reporting; detention as leverage to force retraction; prolonged incommunicado holds designed to extract sources; newsroom raids to seize footage; and, most devastatingly, the targeting of the organizations that support journalists rather than only the journalists themselves.

The Abdalle Mumin case illustrates the last of these most clearly. According to the SJS and RFK Human Rights, his three documented detentions were followed by the court-ordered freezing of the SJS bank accounts. According to the IPI, this represented a coordinated effort against Somalia’s primary press freedom organization: the personal detention of its leader combined with the targeting of its finances. According to all three organizations, no investigation was initiated into any of it.

In April 2024, according to the CPJ, NISA arrested independent journalist Hussein Abdulle Ahmed within days of him publishing an investigation into the dismissal of NISA officials and a second report about an abandoned well allegedly used by security forces as a mass grave. According to the CPJ, he was held for approximately twenty-four hours without charge and released. The message was legible without anyone having to say it aloud.

The silence the numbers cannot capture

The most significant consequence of systematic arbitrary detention is one that no monitoring organisation can fully document: self-censorship. For every journalist arrested and released, colleagues see what happened and they recalibrated. The investigation not pursued. The source not contacted. The paragraph that mattered most, removed from the final report. These absences do not appear on any press freedom index. They disappear in silence — and in this context, silence is not absence. It is a product.

Somalia cannot build accountability without a press capable of independently documenting what its government does. A citizenry without accurate, independent information about the decisions being made in its name cannot hold its decision-makers responsible. The suppression of journalism is therefore not only a violation of journalists’ rights under Article 19 of Somalia’s own constitution. It is a violation of every Somali citizen’s right to know, under Article 18 of that same document.

Somalia’s Provisional Constitution guarantees freedom of the press. In practice, according to multiple independent monitoring organizations, it is not enforced. Human Rights Watch, in its 2023 analysis of the NISA Act, documented that the law grants the agency sweeping powers of arrest, detention, and surveillance with what HRW characterized as minimal independent oversight, and that its broad wording risks being used to suppress the political opposition and media. The US State Department has documented across multiple annual reports what it characterises as a strong and widespread culture of impunity within Somalia’s security forces. According to available records, no security force officer has been prosecuted for the illegal detention of a journalist across the entire period documented in this article.

Three specific actions are required. First, Somalia’s Attorney General should initiate criminal investigations into the most serious documented cases — beginning with the three detentions of Abdalle Ahmed Mumin — to establish that the arbitrary detention of journalists in Somalia does carry legal consequences. Second, the Somali Parliament should enact a dedicated Press Freedom Law explicitly prohibiting arrest on the basis of published content and requiring judicial authorisation for any journalist detention exceeding twenty-four hours. Finally, International partners who fund Somalia’s security sector — including NISA — must make documented progress on press freedom benchmarks a formal condition of that funding: continued support without accountability requirements carries its own share of responsibility for the silencing that follows.

The journalists who did not stop

According to documentation by the SJS, CPJ, IPI, Human Rights Watch, and the US State Department, more than 200 journalists were arbitrarily arrested or detained in Somalia by government security forces between 2019 and 2026. In that same period, according to the same organizations, not one security force officer was prosecuted for illegally detaining a journalist.

Abdalle Ahmed Mumin was detained three times in thirteen months, held for thirty-three days, and subjected to treatment he has publicly described as torture, while, according to the IPI and SJS, the organisation he leads was targeted financially. According to the IPI and SJS, no one was held accountable for any of it. He continues to serve as Secretary-General of the Somali Journalists Syndicate. He continues to document.

Somalia’s constitution promises its citizens a free press. Its journalists are doing everything in their power — at costs that should not be required of them — to be that press. The gap between the constitutional promise and the documented reality is measured in arrests, deleted footage, frozen bank accounts, and thirty-three days in a NISA detention facility for the act of issuing a press statement. That gap is a political choice. The question is whether Somalia’s government, its parliament, and its international partners will finally take seriously what those journalists are risking their lives to document.

title: Amid Growing Fears of Rogue AI, Expert Urges Governments to "Bring This to a Grinding Halt"
content: Is AI superintelligence inevitable? AI safety researcher David Krueger says it doesn’t have to be. Krueger, an assistant professor at the University of Montreal and founder of the nonprofit Evitable, warns that “we need to mitigate the risk of extinction” with regulation and moratoriums to halt the development of AI’s computational power and complexity, which he says is progressing at a rate much faster than current levels of human supervision can manage. Public statements from AI companies that their models have circumvented test constraints and broken into other systems are “what we should expect to happen with the way that we’re building AI, with how little we understand it and how primitive our techniques are for controlling it,” Krueger says. “We just don’t know how to build it safely. End of story.”

title: The dilemma of the ‘undeserving’: Families cut off from food subsidies describe prohibitively complex appeal process
content:
Walaa Mahdi, a resident of a Cairo neighborhood, is among the hundreds of thousands of people across the country who have found their government ration cards suddenly suspended this summer.

The smart card normally gives her and her family access to a basket of household essentials at state-subsidized prices: they get sugar, rice and oil via the card, as well as a daily quota of subsidized loaves.

When her card was suspended, she went to the local supply office to check its status. There, she discovered that her card was suspended on the grounds that her youngest son is enrolled in a private high school.

Mahdi was shocked by the suspension. The school is not a luxury for her son, but a hard-won investment their family is making in his education. They will pay the annual fee in installments, and her son is working alongside his studies to pay for the education. “How can this mean I am ‘underserving’ of support?” she wonders, speaking to Mada Masr.

Mahdi is not alone. She is one of at least 850,000 people the state has expelled from the subsidy program since June in a campaign it is pitching as “purifying operations” to rid the subsidy database of “undeserving” beneficiaries to improve the targeting of government resources.

Amid an outcry over the mass expulsions from citizens and their representatives in parliament, the Supply and Internal Trade Ministry has announced that families can appeal their cards’ suspension. The minister himself appeared on television last week to say that the appeals could be submitted at post offices, local supply offices and via the Digital Egypt platform for grievances, boasting the accuracy of the ministry’s ‘purification’ process by noting that only 2,600 appeals had been submitted so far.

But many of the families, as well as people working to support families’ appeal submissions, tell Mada Masr that even though they believe the expulsions have taken place in error, they have been unable to submit an appeal. They described the process as arduous, complex and bureaucratic.

As they and other families are suddenly pushed outside the support system, their exclusion has sparked concern that the government’s drive to purge “the undeserving” from the database will push households on the brink of coping further into economic difficulty and out of the scope of state protection.

Mahdi’s complaint is similar to that of Selim*, another Cairo resident who spoke to Mada Masr.

In his case, before the recent campaign, not all of his family were registered on the ration card, and for those who were registered, only some were entitled to receive general food subsidies, while others were only entitled only to receive a daily ration of subsidized bread.

Selim said that his card was suspended in recent weeks on the grounds that one of his sons was enrolled in a private school.

But while the government’s list of criteria says that families will be expelled if they pay school fees over LE20,000 per year, the fees for the private school his family member is enrolled in are no more than LE9,800 per year.

Enrolment of one or more children at a private or international school was among one of several criteria for suspending ration cards that the prime minister confirmed during a press conference in July. Other criteria include owning a “modern” car, residing at an upscale residential compound, owning a registered company and having a registered electricity consumption offense or receiving a government pension.

Ahmed, another resident speaking to Mada Masr, described finding his ration card suspended under the car ownership criteria, even though they sold their car years ago. Many on social media describe finding they have been disqualified for registered electricity offenses, even though they have been acquitted of those charges.

Mada Masr spoke with two people who have come across dozens of these cases. They work to provide digital and administrative services to residents in their local area for a fee, such as supporting families to file grievances, complete digital services like updating data or issuing birth certificates.

One of these service-providers in Sohag, Zain al-Abideen, explained that a majority of the people who have approached him about their ration card suspensions in recent weeks have been disqualified because of the private school enrollment criterion.

He also confirmed that while there are many complainants, only a few of them have got as far as submitting the formal appeal.

title: Why Ethiopia’s Conflicts Keep Returning: The Question Ethiopia’s National Dialogue Cannot Avoid
content:
As Ethiopia’s National Dialogue seeks to chart a path toward peace, it faces an immense task. The Dialogue aims to address some of the country’s most difficult political, historical, institutional, social, and peacebuilding questions. Yet its success may ultimately depend on confronting a more basic question: why do Ethiopia’s major conflicts keep returning?

Ethiopia’s National Dialogue Conference, Addis Ababa, 15 July 2026

A problem relocated, not resolved

One answer lies in a problem that has received too little attention. The challenge of nation-building was not resolved after 1991; it was relocated. As political authority came to be organised through ethnoregional states, regional governments became central arenas for managing recognition, representation, and self-government.

This is not an argument against recognition or self-government. Recognition and autonomy expanded opportunities for political participation, representation, and self-rule. But they also changed the way political competition worked. Regional governments became more than administrative units. Through language policy, education, administration, media, public narratives, and territorial claims, regional institutions have often created hierarchies of belonging rather than equal citizenship, making some citizens appear more native, legitimate, or entitled than others. Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts are therefore not only about power. They are also about a system that made identity, territory, representation, and authority increasingly hard to separate.

As these institutions matured, political competition increasingly centred on the representation and defence of communities defined by territory and identity. Contests over leadership, resources, or administration have become securitized struggles over status, belonging, and political survival. While institutions do not cause violence by themselves, they can encourage political actors to present territorial control as a matter of group survival. Losing political power is often experienced not simply as an electoral setback, but as a threat to a group’s place in the political order.

Wolkait, and what it really reveals

This becomes clearest where territory intersects with competing claims of belonging and authority. The Wolkait conflict illustrates the point. Although often presented as a conflict over administrative boundaries, it also reflects deeper questions about membership, government, and the political meaning of territory. Historical claims, constitutional arrangements, ethno-linguistic boundaries, land grievances, displacement, and Ethiopia’s post-1991 regional order all matter. But they do not fully explain why Wolkait became so politically consequential.

The conflict is also about political belonging: who is treated as native, who is seen as a recent settler, and whose authority is considered legitimate. For many Tigrayans, Wolkait’s incorporation into Tigray became part of regional self-government. For many Amharas, it symbolised exclusion from land they regard as historically theirs. It is therefore not only about maps or legal status. It is also about land, memory, identity, representation, and authority.

Wolkait is not an isolated case. Similar patterns appear elsewhere, even when the histories and grievances differ. Addis Ababa offers another example. Its layered history and diverse population show how difficult it is to fit lived belonging into a single ethnic-territorial frame. The continuing conflicts involving the Oromo Liberation Army, an armed Oromo insurgent group, and Fano, a loosely organised Amhara militia movement, illustrate how struggles over security, recognition, and authority become tied to claims about belonging.

Persistent insecurity, displacement crises, and identity-targeted violence across Ethiopia point to a deeper problem. When authority is tied closely to identity and land, basic questions of residence and administration become politically explosive. Politics becomes less about policy or public services, and more about membership, recognition, and control over political space. The human-rights costs can be severe for many citizens, but they are especially acute for people seen as outsiders in the places they live.

This deeper tension is not new. For much of the post-1991 period, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front, or EPRDF, contained it through elite bargaining, central control, and a powerful security apparatus. But containment was not resolution. When the EPRDF-led system began to unravel, the war in Tigray and continuing conflicts in Oromia and Amhara exposed contradictions that had accumulated over decades.

The current government inherited this unresolved tension. Its language of national unity, expressed through the Prosperity Party and Medemer, Abiy Ahmed’s philosophy of political synergy and national togetherness, suggests that it recognises the need to rebuild Ethiopia as a shared political community and marks a departure from the previous EPRDF-led system. But this language has not been matched by a clear institutional answer to the regional ethnic-based identity projects that still shape politics on the ground, nor has a shared citizenship identity taken firm root across the country, where national belonging often competes with stronger ethnic, regional, and territorial claims. Pressured by opposition forces, armed movements, and parts of its own ruling-party base, the government has shifted between containing territorialised identity politics, appeasing it, and at times using it tactically.

What the Dialogue must confront

This is why the National Dialogue matters. Its formal agenda touches many of Ethiopia’s deepest divisions. To contribute to durable peace, the Dialogue must confront the institutional arrangements that turn questions of membership, authority, and land into repeated political crises.

Addressing this problem does not require abandoning federalism. It requires reconsidering how regional states function within it. The problem is not ethnic identification itself, which is normal in diverse societies. The challenge arises when regional institutions become the main arenas where these identifications are politicised, organised, defended, and fought over. In such cases, ethnic and political minorities within regions can face insecurity, discrimination, violence and rights violations. Politics then hardens around exclusion rather than citizenship, deepening tensions between ethnic-based regional loyalty and a shared Ethiopian political project.

This also raises a practical question: where should administrative and political belonging be organised? One answer lies in strengthening institutions below the regional level, including zonal, district (woreda), and municipal governments. Regional states can continue to protect language, culture, and self-government without remaining the principal centres of political loyalty, representation, and authority. They should also play a more active role in reconciling regional and national forms of belonging rather than reinforcing them as competing projects. Stronger sub-regional institutions could broaden representation, accommodate diversity within regions, and sustain multiple and overlapping identities within a common political order.

Such reforms would likely face resistance from actors who see existing arrangements as hard-won guarantees of identity, recognition, and self-rule, including local and diaspora ethnonationalist activists and some influential constituencies within the Prosperity Party itself. Some may argue that democratisation is the real answer. But democracy also requires shared citizenship, trust in common institutions, and a political space where opponents are not treated as threats to the group. Their concerns should be taken seriously, but they should also explain how their positions advance peace and equal citizenship rather than deepen fragmentation.

Regional states are themselves diverse, with strong local identities and histories that cannot always be neatly mapped onto a single ethnic-territorial frame. Yet ethnonationalist projects often seek to flatten these differences by promoting a single ethnic narrative and pushing for more homogeneous political communities. Ethiopia needs institutions that preserve diversity while strengthening equal citizenship, national cohesion, and a shared political future.

This does not mean that federalism was a mistake. It means recognition alone is insufficient. Ethiopians already recognise their differences. The challenge is whether those differences can coexist within institutions that sustain a common political future and prevent competing forms of belonging from becoming competing centres of political authority.

The implications extend beyond Ethiopia. For much of the post 1991 period, international partners viewed Ethiopia’s federal order through the lenses of recognition, inclusion, self-government, and conflict management, while paying less attention to the risks of regional institutions becoming vehicles for separate political projects. Once consolidated, these projects make reform harder and conflict easier to mobilise. They encourage political actors, including armed groups, to frame control over territory, institutions, and identity as matters of security, dignity, and political belonging. For a country as central to the Horn of Africa as Ethiopia, this is not only a domestic issue, but also a question of regional stability. Ethnic identity-based mobilisation can deepen exclusion, fuel armed competition, and create forces that are difficult to control.

That is why the National Dialogue must go beyond questions of constitutional design or power distribution alone. Whether Ethiopia amends the constitution, replaces it, reforms federal institutions, or retains the current system, none of these options will be enough unless the Dialogue confronts the deeper problem. Ethiopia’s shared future depends on turning its entangled identities, histories, territories, and forms of belonging into grounds for equal citizenship rather than conflict. The real test is whether Ethiopia’s political actors, especially ethnonationalist forces at home and abroad, including those in power, are ready to make recognition and self-government serve peace and a common political future rather than separate and competing political projects.

title: Nonviolent Citizen Resistance Moves the World Social Forum Forward in Benin
content:
By Guy Feugap, Africa Organizer, World BEYOND War, August 5, 2026

After a long period of uncertainty that raised fears of the cancellation of the 2026 World Social Forum, the Government of Benin finally authorized this important gathering of social movements to take place. World BEYOND War welcomes this decision and the power of nonviolent action by civil society.

The African Organizer of World BEYOND War arrived in Cotonou on August 3, 2026, to contribute to the Forum through several initiatives, including the official launch of the World BEYOND War Benin chapter and a series of international dialogues on war in Sudan. The Forum’s opening march, along with other activities planned at the official venue, could not take place because of a last-minute cancellation by the Government of Benin. These events are regrettable at a time when Africa is facing armed conflicts, humanitarian crises, and growing militarization. Spaces for dialogue, cooperation, and peacebuilding such as the World Social Forum are more necessary than ever. It is paradoxical that a continent suffering so deeply from the consequences of war should trivialize a gathering dedicated to peace and international solidarity.

Faced with this situation, the participating organizations did not give into discouragement. They multiplied consultations, coordinated their positions, and continued their exchanges in a spirit of solidarity and nonviolence. This calm and determined mobilization helped maintain pressure in favor of holding the Forum and reminded everyone of the importance of respecting civic freedoms and spaces for dialogue.

The decision of the Beninese authorities to finally authorize the Forum is an encouraging signal. It shows that peaceful citizen mobilization can produce concrete results. This development represents a victory for the organizations present in Cotonou, and also for all those who believe in the power of nonviolent action to defend rights, democracy, and peace.

title: Volunteer Spotlight: Baltimore Chapter Co-Coordinator Ronda Cooperstein
content:
Each month, we share the stories of World BEYOND War volunteers around the world. Want to volunteer with World BEYOND War? Email greta@worldbeyondwar.org.

I became an anti-war activist at a young age, after reading many books about Indigenous peoples across the globe. I was shocked and appalled at the violence inflicted on so many innocent populations in the name of civilization. Once in college, in the late 70’s, I became active on campus, joining and supporting groups that worked for peace and justice. As a Jewish American, I became very active in issues related to Israel/Palestine and went on to found a local organization, Baltimore Jews for Israeli Palestinian Peace. After years and years of working locally on these issues, I decided to start a chapter of World BEYOND War in Baltimore. I was inspired by the Ukrainian conscientious objector, Yurii Sheliazhenko, who is a Board Member of World BEYOND War.

Our local chapter, since forming a little over a year ago, has worked mainly on issues related to Israel/Palestine, hosting Combatants for Peace, bringing Israeli genocide scholar Omer Bartov to Baltimore, and holding vigils. We also lobby our Congress members to support all anti-war legislation and to take a stand against militarism at all levels. Last summer we co-sponsored the local Hiroshima/Nagasaki Memorial event. In the fall, we will be bringing WBW Co-Founder and Executive Director David Swanson to Baltimore.

My top recommendation for someone who wants to get involved is to remember that no act on behalf of peace is too small, that every person counts, that kindness and solidarity at all levels are the keys to moving forward.

What keeps me inspired is knowing that we are responsible for one another, for the Earth and all its inhabitants, human and non-human. Therefore, the extraordinary violence and cruelty of the U.S. government and its allies can never be ignored.

title: “La tierra no se vende, no se quema ni se desaloja”: Jornada Federal contra la extranjerización de la tierra
content:
Este jueves 6 de agosto, mientras el Senado se disponga a debatir la denominada “Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada”, un amplio marco de organizaciones campesinas, indígenas, ambientales, sociales, políticas, de derechos humanos y sindicales realizarán una jornada federal de protesta en distintos puntos del país. La convocatoria central será frente al Congreso Nacional, bajo la consigna “La tierra no se vende, no se quema ni se desaloja”, en rechazo a un proyecto que denuncian como un nuevo avance sobre los territorios y los bienes comunes. La jornada incluirá una radio abierta, un “verdurazo” y un festival cultural. También habrá acciones en otros puntos del mundo, como Berlín (Alemania). Las organizaciones sostienen que la iniciativa legislativa se inscribe en una política de profundización del extractivismo y de apertura al capital extranjero que, junto al RIGI y otras reformas impulsadas por el gobierno de Javier Milei, amenaza con acelerar los desalojos, la concentración de la tierra y la pérdida de soberanía territorial.

Mientras el Senado se prepara para debatir este jueves 6 de agosto la denominada Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada, organizaciones indígenas, campesinas, ambientales, sociales, políticas, sindicales y de derechos humanos convocan a una jornada federal de movilización para rechazar una iniciativa que consideran un nuevo avance sobre los territorios, los bienes comunes y la soberanía nacional.

Las actividades comenzarán hoy, miércoles 5 de agosto a las 12, con un “Culturazo en defensa de la tierra y la soberanía” y una conferencia de prensa en el Teatro Picadero (Pasaje Enrique Santos Discépolo 1857, CABA), impulsada de forma conjunta por la Coordinadora Plurinacional Basta de Falsas Soluciones (BFS), Actrices Argentinas, el Colectivo de Acción por la Justicia Ecosocial (CAJE) y la Asociación Argentina de Abogados/as Ambientalistas. Allí, las organizaciones presentarán públicamente los fundamentos de su rechazo al proyecto, sosteniendo que la ley forma parte de un paquete de reformas que favorecen la concentración de la tierra, profundizan los desalojos y fortalecen un modelo basado en el extractivismo y la mercantilización de los bienes comunes.

En tanto, bajo la consigna “La tierra no se vende, no se quema, ni se desaloja”, este jueves 6 de agosto la convocatoria central será desde el mediodía frente al Congreso Nacional, donde habrá radio abierta, un festival cultural, un “verdurazo” y distintas intervenciones durante toda la jornada.

También, desde las 18 tendrá lugar frente al Congreso Nacional el “Festival en Lucha”, con la participación Willy Bronca y Malena D’Alessio, que contará también con la lectura de un documento conjunto a cargo de Charo López, Juan Solá, Maite Lanata, Jazmín Stuart y Adolfo Pérez Esquivel.

Ver esta publicación en Instagram Una publicación compartida por Coordinadora Plurinacional BFS (@bastadefalsassoluciones)

De la movilización al Congreso Nacional también participarán desde la Confederación de Combatientes de Malvinas por considerar que “el proyecto impulsado por el gobierno nacional se trata de una claudicación de soberanía sin precedentes” y que “este gobierno maltrata a su pueblo, agobia a sus jubilados, quita educación y salud, y no cuestiona que magnates como Benetton, Lewis y otros grandes grupos económicos continúen expropiándose vastas extensiones de la Argentina”. En ese sentido, remarcan: “la doble vara es evidente: se ataca lo publico y se protege la concentracion y extranjerizacion de la tierra”.

Quienes ofrecieron su vida y su integridad física en defensa de nuestras Islas Malvinas en 1982 acaban de lanzar un comunicado afirmando que van a marchar este 6 de agosto en contra de la ley y en defensa de nuestro territorio y los recursos naturales pic.twitter.com/RKL61bafaG — Rattenbach (@jmrosas1845) August 4, 2026

Las movilizaciones y acciones tendrán alcance nacional. Además de la protesta frente al Congreso Nacional mientras el Senado esté tratando el proyecto, habrá actividades en varias localidades del país, como Baradero, Mar del Plata, Rosario, Córdoba, Mendoza, Tucumán, La Pampa, Jujuy, Salta, Bariloche (Río Negro), Comarca Andina (Chubut), Posadas (Misiones), Paraná (Entre Ríos) y Ushuaia, Río Grande y Tolhuin (Tierra del Fuego), según relevó la cuenta de instagram de Rebelión o Extinción .

A estas movilizaciones y acciones se suman también:

La Plata: semaforazo a las 17 en 7 y 50.

Chubut: concentración desde las 17 en la Plaza Independencia de Trelew, en la Plaza San Martín de Puerto Madryn desde las 18 y en la Plaza Kompuchewe de Comodoro Rivadavia desde las 12.

San Juan: concentración en la Plaza 25 de Mayo.

San Luis Capital: concentración en el Correo Argentino desde las 17.

Neuquén: en el Monumento a San Martín de Neuquén desde las 17 y concentración en la Plaza Pioneros a las 18 para una posterior movilización.

Entre Ríos: en la Plaza San Martín de Colón desde las 19 y en la Plaza Ramírez de Concepción del Uruguay desde las 18.

Chaco: en la Plaza 25 de Mayo de Resistencia desde las 17.

Santa Fe: concentración en El Molino Fábrica Cultural en Santa Fe Capital desde las 17.

Corrientes Capital: en la Plaza 25 de Mayo a las 16.

La jornada de movilización y lucha se replicará en otros puntos del mundo, como es el caso de la convocatoria de la Asamblea en Solidaridad con Argentina en Berlín para el jueves 6 de agosto a las 16.30 en la Puerta de Brandeburgo (Berlín, Alemania).

Ver esta publicación en Instagram Una publicación compartida por Asamblea en Solidaridad con Argentina en Berlin (@argentinanosevende.berlin)

Un intento de avanzar con la pérdida de soberanía a espaldas de la población

Este jueves 6 de agosto, el gobierno de Javier Milei y sectores de la oposición dialoguista buscarán reunir los votos necesarios para aprobar este avance sobre la soberanía nacional. En este marco, ¿quiénes son las y los senadores que votarán a favor de la extranjerización de la tierra? Conocelos uno por uno:

¿Quiénes son las y los senadores que votarán a favor de la extranjerización de la tierra?

La discusión parlamentaria se produce en un contexto de creciente cuestionamiento social al avance de la extranjerización de la tierra. De hecho, un reciente relevamiento de la consultora Zuban Córdoba arrojó que un 77% de las y los argentinos consultados está en contra de la ley y a favor de limitar la compra de tierras por parte de extranjeros y considera que el Estado debe preservar el control nacional sobre los recursos estratégicos. Ese escenario contrasta con el impulso que el Gobierno nacional busca darle al proyecto en el Senado.

Ver esta publicación en Instagram Una publicación compartida por Vanina Biasi (@vaninabiasi)

En los últimos meses, ANRed documentó distintos conflictos que anticipan el impacto que podría tener esta legislación: desde el avance de grandes grupos económicos sobre tierras en Misiones, Corrientes y Entre Ríos hasta los procesos de desplazamiento de comunidades campesinas e indígenas, y la creciente presión sobre territorios rurales y costeros, esta agencia registró cómo la disputa por la tierra se encuentra estrechamente vinculada con el modelo extractivo impulsado desde el Estado.

El Paraná en venta: cómo avanza la extranjerización de la tierra en Misiones, Corrientes y Entre Ríos

Del Requerimiento a la Propiedad Inviolable

En esa línea, Julia Strada, directora del Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA) y Diputada Nacional por UxP, calificó en su cuenta de X como “una trampa” la propuesta de llevar el límite del 15% actual al supuesto 25% para la compra de tierras que está negociando el gobierno con varios gobernadores para lograr los votos necesarios para que la ley sea votada en el Senado.

En esa línea, enumeró la riqueza natural en departamentos que podrían extranjerizarse al 100% con la propuesta del gobierno, ya que igual seguirían por debajo del límite del 25% del territorio provincial).

EL GOBIERNO INSISTE CON VENDER EL PAÍS: EL SUPUESTO LÍMITE DEL 25% EN LA LEY DE EXTRANJERIZACIÓN DE TIERRAS ES UNA TRAMPA Te muestro algunas imágenes de la riqueza natural en departamentos que podrían extranjerizarse al 100% con la propuesta del gobierno (ya que igual seguirían… pic.twitter.com/GN6tLTwN2W — Julia Strada (@Juli_Strada) August 4, 2026

En este marco, las organizaciones que convocan a la jornada sostienen que la ley no puede analizarse de manera aislada. La vinculan con el Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI), con la expansión de proyectos mineros, petroleros y forestales, con el avance sobre territorios indígenas y la flexibilización de normas que históricamente buscaron limitar la concentración y extranjerización de la tierra. Desde esa perspectiva, advierten que el proyecto consolida un marco jurídico favorable para los grandes capitales en detrimento de quienes habitan y producen en esos territorios.

La protesta también se inscribe en un escenario de creciente conflictividad social marcado por el ajuste económico, los recortes presupuestarios y la profundización de las políticas acordadas con el Fondo Monetario Internacional. Para las organizaciones convocantes, la apertura irrestricta a las inversiones extranjeras y la desregulación sobre la propiedad de la tierra forman parte de una misma estrategia que prioriza la obtención de divisas mediante el extractivismo, aun a costa del deterioro ambiental, la pérdida de soberanía y el desplazamiento de comunidades.

En este contexto, la jornada del 6 de agosto buscará transformar el debate parlamentario en una discusión pública sobre el futuro del territorio argentino. Así, frente a un modelo que profundiza el saqueo de los bienes comunes y favorece la concentración económica, las organizaciones proponen fortalecer la defensa de la tierra, el agua y los territorios como bienes colectivos indispensables para la soberanía, la producción de alimentos y la vida de las comunidades que los habitan.

title: Violência de gênero virou pauta eleitoral. Mas ainda falta coragem
content:
No título do seu último livro, a filósofa Judith Butler lança uma pergunta: “Quem tem medo de gênero?”. Butler, que é uma das maiores referências nos estudos de gênero, no feminismo contemporâneo e na teoria queer, fala sobre como o “gênero” se tornou peça central para os discursos conservadores e reacionários, um fantasma com o objetivo de criar pânico moral e conseguir apoio popular a projetos políticos fascistas, autoritários e excludentes. É um livro muito bom que eu indico fortemente, sobretudo para quem não tem familiaridade com o assunto ou nunca leu Butler; é seu primeiro livro não acadêmico.

Diante desta pergunta, a pesquisadora brasileira Sônia Corrêa, coordenadora do Observatório de Sexualidade e Política, costuma responder com uma provocação: “Quem tem medo de gênero é a esquerda, a extrema direita odeia gênero”.

Sim, temos evidências disso ao longo da história do país. Do ódio, acho que nem preciso falar aqui. E para provar o medo, temos de cartas assinadas por candidatos se comprometendo a não descriminalizar o aborto a declarações dúbias e escorregadias em debates televisionados e mudanças de planos de governo feitas de última hora para agradar pastores evangélicos. Sobretudo o aborto, mas também questões relacionadas a proteção e avanço nos direitos da comunidade LGBTQ+, são temas que as campan has eleitorais presidenciais de esquerda e centro esquerda tendem a evitar. Ou, pior, um tema para se “rifar” facilmente.

Esse ano, no entanto, a pauta da violência de gênero se tornou difícil de ser evitada pelos candidatos. O ano começou com feminicídios, tentativas de feminicídios, mutilações, crimes cometidos contra crianças e bebês estampando os jornais – coisas da ordem do horror absoluto. Os números do Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública , divulgados recentemente, também são assombrosos. Enquanto as mortes violentas seguem em queda contínua há cinco anos, os feminicídios no Brasil bateram recorde em 2025. Foram 1.571 feminicídios ao longo do ano passado. Isso significa 4 mulheres mortas por dia. Também aumentaram os números de tentativas de feminicídio, violência psicológica, descumprimento de medida protetiva, ameaças, stalking, posse ou distribuição de conteúdos de abuso sexual infantil e violência doméstica. Os dados mais recentes do Atlas da Violência também indicam que os registros de violência contra pessoas LGBTQ+ no Brasil seguem crescendo e, apesar de não haver uma pesquisa oficial sobre isso, organizações brasileiras e internacionais apontam o Brasil como o país que mais mata pessoas trans no mundo.

Ao mesmo tempo em que essa violência cresce, pesquisas têm mostrado que no Brasil e no mundo as mulheres tendem a votar mais em partidos de esquerda e centro-esquerda. Mas tem um detalhe importante: segundo dados do TSE desse ano, as mulheres são 52% do eleitorado brasileiro. Ou seja, nem precisa ser bom em matemática para entender que esses votos são cada vez mais importantes. Michelle Bolsonaro entendeu e fez Flávio entender. O PL entendeu. Lula certamente tem entendido, como mostram ações de governo e falas recentes.

Entre os candidatos (quase todos homens) propostas para “acabar com a violência contra a mulher” já estão pipocando e devem ter um lugar importante nos debates e planos de governo em 2026. Já não era sem tempo.

A maioria das propostas até agora têm ido na direção do endurecimento da repressão.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) fala em castração química para estupradores e em defender as mulheres “com força”. Como se o estupro viesse de um desejo incontrolável e biológico e não de uma relação de poder e a subjugação de corpos que são vistos como inferiores, mais fracos, propriedade privada. O candidato fala a partir da visão do macho salvador que protege “com força”.

Romeu Zema, defendendo que a política precisa de mais mulheres, associou a atuação política feminina a uma característica biológica. “A mulher, por natureza, por uma questão biológica, ela pensa no futuro. Porque quando ela engravida, ela vai ter um projeto ali de, no mínimo, 15 anos. E o homem não tem essa visão.” Ao mesmo tempo, o candidato à presidência pelo Novo se posicionou contra o PL da Misoginia, projeto de lei que altera a Lei Antirracismo para incluir os chamados atos de misoginia, definidos como “a prática, a indução ou a incitação de menosprezo ou discriminação contra a mulher, que promova violência, negue sua igualdade de direitos ou ofenda sua dignidade, em razão da condição de mulher”.

Assim como os demais, Lula também tem defendido o aumento da pena para o crime de feminicídio. Recentemente declarou em um evento: “Nós estamos fazendo o Pacto contra o Feminicídio. E vamos endurecer. O cidadão que bater na mulher vai ter que ser punido, vai ter que utilizar tornozeleira e, se a mulher quiser, não vai nem encostar mais nela. E aumentar a pena para quem mata mulher. Não é possível o cidadão trancar a mulher e o filho em casa e tocar fogo, o cidadão dar 66 socos na cara da mulher”. Com relação à pauta do aborto o presidente é ambíguo. Já declarou ser pessoalmente contra a prática, e indicou ao STF Jorge Messias, que se declara “totalmente contra o aborto”. Mas diz que o tema precisa ser tratado como questão de saúde pública pelo Estado e criticou propostas para endurecer penas de mulheres que abortam. O presidente também sancionou a lei de igualdade salarial entre homens e mulheres e iniciou o governo com número recorde de 11 ministras, além de ter criado o Bolsa Família, que é indubitavelmente uma porta de saída para mulheres em situação de violência doméstica.

As principais propostas até agora têm focado em medidas de punição e não de prevenção. Quando um homem é punido, a violência já aconteceu . Enquanto isso, nas escolas, as discussões sobre machismo, LGBTfobia, masculinidades, seguem sendo censuradas. Os influencers redpill e as comunidades incel seguem sendo menosprezadas. Os crimes virtuais seguem num limbo. A pauta do aborto segue chegando à população apenas pela lente do crime ou do pecado. E as discussões sobre questões de gênero seguem “delicadas”, não atravessadas pela pauta antirracista como deveriam e não sendo enfrentadas pelas esquerdas que estão no poder.

Você consegue imaginar um candidato dizendo em um debate na TV que o Brasil tem que parar de matar pessoas trans? Ou defender que a descriminalização do aborto é uma questão de saúde pública?

Não basta encarar “as pautas de mulheres” como aquele chefe que no dia 08 de março dá um bombom sonho de valsa com um papel rosa grampeado dizendo “mulher, você é especial”, mas segue pagando menos às funcionárias. É fácil dizer que é contra a violência doméstica. A gente precisa de mais. Falta coragem aos candidatos homens para tratar desta séria discussão.
